reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: An X-linked proximal tubulopathy that mainly affects males, characterised by low-molecular-weight proteinuria, hypercalciuria, and progressive kidney impairment
Most cases (Dent disease 1) arise from mutations in CLCN5 encoding a chloride/proton exchanger; a minority (Dent disease 2) result from OCRL1 mutations that overlap with Lowe syndrome
Recurrent calcium-containing stones and nephrocalcinosis are common and may be the presenting feature in childhood or early adulthood
Low-molecular-weight proteinuria (e.g. retinol-binding protein, beta-2-microglobulin) is a consistent and useful diagnostic marker
Additional features of proximal tubular dysfunction may appear, such as glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, and a partial Fanconi picture
Female carriers are usually mild or asymptomatic but may show hypercalciuria or low-grade low-molecular-weight proteinuria
Management is supportive, aiming to reduce hypercalciuria and stone burden and to slow progression, since no specific curative therapy exists
Progression to kidney failure typically occurs between the third and fifth decades in affected males
reference.pathophysiology: Dent disease is an inherited disorder of proximal tubular endosomal function. Loss-of-function mutations in CLCN5 (Dent disease 1) impair the chloride/proton antiporter needed for endosomal acidification and receptor-mediated endocytosis, disrupting reabsorption of filtered low-molecular-weight proteins and altering handling of calcium and other solutes. OCRL1 mutations (Dent disease 2) affect a phosphatidylinositol phosphatase and produce an overlapping phenotype. The resulting defective endocytosis leads to low-molecular-weight proteinuria, hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis and stones, and eventual tubulointerstitial damage with declining kidney function.
additionalDifferentials: Cystinuria and other hereditary stone disorders
Other causes of renal Fanconi syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Quantification of low-molecular-weight proteinuria (e.g. retinol-binding protein or beta-2-microglobulin)
Renal ultrasound to detect nephrocalcinosis and stones
Assessment of proximal tubular function (urine glucose, amino acids, phosphate)
Genetic testing for CLCN5 and OCRL1 mutations
redFlags: Progressive decline in kidney function toward kidney failure
Recurrent obstructing stones with pain or infection
Growth impairment or rickets in children from tubular phosphate wasting
reference.prognosis: Kidney function declines gradually, and many affected males reach kidney failure in mid-adult life; extrarenal outcomes are otherwise generally favourable, and carrier females typically remain mildly affected.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis in a young male with recurrent stones by not testing for low-molecular-weight proteinuria
Attributing the picture to idiopathic hypercalciuria and missing the underlying tubulopathy
Failing to recognise the overlap with Lowe syndrome in OCRL1-related disease
Assuming carrier females are always unaffected
